{"id": "23:72/q05", "question": "How are خرج and خراج distinguished?", "turns_on": "The notes differ over synonymy, the breadth of the two terms, and whether the contrast is obligation, payer, timing, grammatical form, or kind of revenue.", "positions": [{"id": "23:72/q05/p1", "position": "They are synonymous or share the basic sense of assessed revenue, produce or recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash says variation of wording is more elegant. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī say both are verbal nouns without plurals, with al-Jishumī deriving them from assessed collection. Al-ʿAṣmaʿī's distinction is usage rather than fundamental meaning according to Ibn ʿAṭiyya; Asad also calls them broadly synonymous. Abū al-Ḥasan could not decide which form is more common."}, {"id": "23:72/q05/p2", "position": "Kharj is a voluntary payment; kharāj is an obligatory due.", "reasons": "Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl transmits this from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ; al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and others report it."}, {"id": "23:72/q05/p3", "position": "Kharj is the narrower human payment, while kharāj is broader or more ample.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī and al-Nasafī argue that extra letters suit greater meaning and the mixed reading. Al-Nasafī compares a village's revenue with Kūfa's levy. Al-Bayḍāwī, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī say land-tax usage evokes abundant recurring income. Qirāʾāt ER contrasts a specific payment with systematic revenue. Asad marks worldly recompense for people but leaves God's unrestricted. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers a broad/narrow distinction over synonymy, though he reports that the wording attributed to al-Zamakhsharī was corrected in al-Farāʾid as quoted by al-Ṭībī."}, {"id": "23:72/q05/p4", "position": "Kharj is the broader term for anything paid out, while kharāj specifically denotes land tax.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī cites al-ʿAjjāj and a poem about land tax; he connects the people's offered gift in 18:94–95 with the general kharj sense. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports an argument attributed to al-Zamakhsharī in this direction and a correction of its reversed wording."}, {"id": "23:72/q05/p5", "position": "Kharj is paid by persons; kharāj comes from land.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ is reported by al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī; Ibn al-Aʿrābī by Ibn ʿĀshūr."}, {"id": "23:72/q05/p6", "position": "Kharj is a fee, while kharāj is a gift or allowance.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥātim gives this distinction in al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī."}, {"id": "23:72/q05/p7", "position": "Kharj is a verbal noun, while kharāj is a substantive noun.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn Yazīd or al-Mubarrad is reported in al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī."}, {"id": "23:72/q05/p8", "position": "Kharj is a one-time payment; kharāj is periodically recurring.", "reasons": "Al-Aṣmaʿī gives the distinction; Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats it as usage while saying the underlying senses coincide."}, {"id": "23:72/q05/p9", "position": "Kharāj is fayʾ, whereas kharj is a tax or jizya.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī transmits the distinction from al-Zajjāj."}, {"id": "23:72/q05/p10", "position": "Both terms can refer to land dues, a worker's wage or stipend, and assessed revenue.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī mentions dues on slave or land; Ibn Maktūm, quoted by al-Biqāʿī, includes annual measured levies on communal wealth and the earnings of a slave or bondwoman. The Kashshāf allows land dues to rulers and workers' pay for either form."}]}
{"id": "23:72/q06", "question": "How are the two payment words read?", "turns_on": "The written or recited presence of alif in each word, and whether matching or contrasting forms convey a nuance.", "positions": [{"id": "23:72/q06/p1", "position": "The first is read without alif and the second with alif: kharjan fa-kharāj.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim and Abū ʿAmr are repeatedly named; al-Jishumī adds Abū Jaʿfar and Yaʿqūb, Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it the majority. Al-Ḥasan is also reported to recite it, and Qirāʾāt ER says it contrasts a specific fee with systematic revenue. Al-Zajjāj reports the alternative with alif in the first word. The Nasafī gives a divergent grouping of readers. Al-Nashr refers back to earlier discussion without restating forms. Al-Naḥḥās and Ibn ʿĀshūr say variation avoids inelegant repetition; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares a more distant repetition in 34:47. Al-Nasafī explicitly prefers the mixed reading for its greater second term."}, {"id": "23:72/q06/p2", "position": "Both are read without alif: kharjan fa-kharj.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀmir is repeatedly named; al-Qurṭubī adds Abū Ḥaywa for the second form. Al-Nasafī instead attributes the second unlengthened form to ʿAlī and Ḥamza. Qirāʾāt ER says this removes the specific-versus-systematic contrast. Ibn ʿĀshūr says repeating a form suits synonymy and paired symmetry."}, {"id": "23:72/q06/p3", "position": "Both are read with alif: kharājan fa-kharāj.", "reasons": "Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī are repeatedly named; Ibn ʿĀshūr adds Khalaf, and al-Qurṭubī adds al-Aʿmash and Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb for the first word. Al-Bayḍāwī cites matched sound patterns. Qirāʾāt ER says both words suggest systematic extraction; Ibn ʿĀshūr says repetition suits synonymy."}, {"id": "23:72/q06/p4", "position": "A reported reversal reads kharājan fa-kharj.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes it to al-Ḥasan and ʿĪsā; he says the first larger term can stress entrenched disbelief and the second, smaller term that even a little from God surpasses much from people."}]}
{"id": "23:72/q07", "question": "What is meant by 'your Lord's kharāj'?", "turns_on": "Whether kharāj here is worldly sustenance, later reward, both, unrestricted recompense, or imposed dues.", "positions": [{"id": "23:72/q07/p1", "position": "It is God's reward or recompense in the Hereafter for the Prophet's obedience and calling.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ḥasan and many others contrast it with worldly wages; al-Qurṭubī reports Quraysh offered to make the Prophet their richest man and he declined. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says reward is called compensation in context. Iṣlāḥī says God supports messengers and righteous successors who preach truth."}, {"id": "23:72/q07/p2", "position": "It is God's worldly sustenance or gift, better than any payment from people.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās calls it His gift; al-Kalbī specifies worldly sustenance. Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites the following 'best provider' as evidence. Al-Bayḍāwī says its breadth and permanence leave the Messenger without need for fees. Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī stress that none grants favor like God."}, {"id": "23:72/q07/p3", "position": "It includes provision in this life and reward in the next, both greater and more lasting than a human fee.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī expressly combine the two. Bursevī says this makes the Messenger independent of gifts; al-Ālūsī adds freedom from obligation to people."}, {"id": "23:72/q07/p4", "position": "In the mixed reading, God's kharāj can point to land dues and capitation He has imposed.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī invokes 25:57 and 12:104, where the Prophet asks no wage, to explain the contrast."}, {"id": "23:72/q07/p5", "position": "It is God's unrestricted recompense, without limiting it to this world or the next.", "reasons": "Asad's translation leaves God's recompense open while marking the human side as worldly."}]}
{"id": "23:72/q08", "question": "Why is God's kharāj better than theirs?", "turns_on": "The usual explanation stresses abundance and permanence; one explanation makes the contrast striking even if God's gift is phrased as small.", "positions": [{"id": "23:72/q08/p1", "position": "God gives more, more reliably and for longer, so the Prophet has no need for their payment.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān contrast even a small human fee with the Creator's greater gift. Al-Bayḍāwī says God's provision is broad and lasting; al-Biqāʿī says His reward is never cut off or withheld even from sinners and 'due' hints at a pledge to provide. Bursevī says His gift never ends or becomes clouded; al-Ālūsī adds freedom from human obligation. Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Ālūsī say the final provider clause reinforces this superiority."}, {"id": "23:72/q08/p2", "position": "Even a little from God is better than much from them.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī offers this explanation for the reported kharājan fa-kharj reading, alongside a stress on the rejecters' entrenched disbelief."}]}
{"id": "23:72/q09", "question": "Why does the verse say 'your Lord'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:72/q09/p1", "position": "It strengthens the argument and honors the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explains the address in this way."}]}
{"id": "23:72/q10", "question": "What does calling God 'the best of providers' imply?", "turns_on": "Whether 'best' bears only on the quality of giving or also yields a rule about what counts as provision.", "positions": [{"id": "23:72/q10/p1", "position": "God gives and rewards best, while created people may provide for one another through His permission and without equalling Him.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī says God allots one person's provision through another's hands; the 'people of meanings,' al-Jubbāʾī and al-Jishumī argue that the comparative presupposes other providers. Al-Wāḥidī cites Arabic usage about a ruler providing for soldiers. Al-Ṭabrisī expressly qualifies human provision by God's permission. Al-Biqāʿī says God knows each recipient's benefit and harm and provides without being asked. Al-Qurṭubī says none bestows favor as He does; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the clause parenthetical praise of His abundant favor."}, {"id": "23:72/q10/p2", "position": "Unlawful things do not count as God's provision.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī draws this inference from saying that God's provision is best."}]}

ons": [{"id": "23:72/q11/p1", "position": "Umm al-Dardāʾ says provision comes through people; accept it, use what is needed and pass surplus to needy brethren.", "reasons": "She says God does not send coins from heaven and warns against rejecting provision He sends."}, {"id": "23:72/q11/p2", "position": "The Prophet told ʿUmar to accept an unsolicited gift, then use it or give it to the needy.", "reasons": "The gift must be neither sought nor pursued."}, {"id": "23:72/q11/p3", "position": "ʿUmar gave Qurayshī ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd a thousand dinars and urged him to accept it.", "reasons": "Qubayṣa ibn Dhuʾayb reports that ʿUmar cited the Prophet's instruction about unsolicited gifts."}, {"id": "23:72/q11/p4", "position": "Bahlūl refused Hārūn's offer to pay his debts or grant a pension.", "reasons": "He reasoned that debt cannot be discharged with debt and that God would not remember Hārūn while forgetting another servant; Bursevī links this to unexpected divine provision being better than a specified human source."}]}
{"id": "23:72/q12", "question": "What practice does the verse suggest for preaching or seeking wages?", "turns_on": "Whether the Prophet's example requires abstention or permits wages while preferring abstention.", "positions": [{"id": "23:72/q12/p1", "position": "A preacher may lawfully take wages, but abstaining is better; prophets chose God's reward.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports Ibn al-ʿArabī's view that preaching wages are among the most lawful earnings."}, {"id": "23:72/q12/p2", "position": "One should preach without seeking payment or trading knowledge for livelihood.", "reasons": "Bursevī quotes a Persian couplet warning that an exegete loses by selling knowledge and skill for bread. {"id": "23:72/q13", "question": "What inward counsel is drawn from the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:72/q13/p1", "position": "Those firmly grounded in knowing God should call people through God without staining their hearts with worldly or otherworldly desires.", "reasons": "Bursevī quotes the Taʾwīlāt Najmiyya."}]}
{"id": "23:72/q14", "question": "How did the Meccan idolaters respond to the Prophet's call?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:72/q14/p1", "position": "They strayed from right belief and conduct despite the Prophet's efforts.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu describes the path he called them to as Islam and says they went astray despite his work."}]}
{"id": "23:73/q01", "question": "Who are the people Muhammad calls?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:73/q01/p1", "position": "Muhammad's own people, identified as the Quraysh disbelievers or Meccan idolaters.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi names the Quraysh disbelievers; Kur'an Yolu calls them Meccan idolaters; the dream reported by Ibn Kathir speaks of the Prophet and his people as travelers."}]}
{"id": "23:73/q02", "question": "What is the straight path to which he calls them?", "turns_on": "Whether the path is identified with Islam and its practice, described through truth and straightness, or read as a spiritual way of following or attainment.", "positions": [{"id": "23:73/q02/p1", "position": "Islam, the upright and sound religion, embracing monotheism, sincere worship, and obedience to religious law.", "reasons": "Muqatil and al-Tha'labi identify it as Islam without crookedness; Yahya ibn Sallam calls it sound religion and the road to Paradise. Al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi call it upright religion and explain that religion is called a road because it leads to Paradise; al-Qurtubi also glosses sirat as road. Al-Wahidi says Muhammad invites the Quraysh disbelievers to Islam; al-Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, and al-Nasafi likewise identify Islam, with al-Nasafi adding that they should answer him. Al-Tabrisi specifies monotheism, sincere worship of God, and action according to religious law. Kur'an Yolu says the Prophet's sole aim is inviting to Islam, for which God will reward him better; it describes the Meccan idolaters as straying from right belief and conduct despite his efforts. Qatada's reported parable in al-Durr depicts invitation to Islam as a familiar guide leading someone from a rough route onto a broad, easy road."}, {"id": "23:73/q02/p2", "position": "A clear, true, consistently straight way without crookedness, leading its followers to their goal.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says proof establishes this way as sound and more fully straight than an ordinary road. Al-Baydawi, al-Bursevi, and al-Alusi say sound minds attest to its straightness and find no deviation that could justify accusing or suspecting the Messenger. Ibn Kathir restates that the Prophet calls to a straight path. Al-Biqa'i says the reminder offers no crookedness or valid flaw and that following it reaches the goal and every honor. Qatada, as reported by al-Durr, glosses it as a path without crookedness. Al-Tabataba'i says truth is one, its parts do not conflict, its judgment is clear and consistent, and it reaches the intended end; because the Prophet guides to truth he guides to this path. Islahi calls it the clear salvation path reaching the true destination, whose following requires belief in the Hereafter; Asad says those denying the afterlife deviate from it."}, {"id": "23:73/q02/p3", "position": "The direct and sound path of following, whose end is disclosed through correctness and truth.", "reasons": "Some authorities reported by al-Sulami describe it as the most direct route to uprightness and emphasize following."}, {"id": "23:73/q02/p4", "position": "Paths of attainment fit for those steadfast with God, seeking none other and claiming no spiritual rank.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata, reported by al-Sulami, says the Prophet leads people on paths of attainment, but only those steadfast with God are fit for that way; they claim neither rank nor station for themselves."}]}
{"id": "23:73/q03", "question": "What pronunciations of ṣirāṭ are reported?", "turns_on": "Phonetic realization of the initial consonant of ṣirāṭ.", "positions": [{"id": "23:73/q03/p1", "position": "Pronounce it with sīn in place of ṣād.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER calls this a phonetic alternation between non-emphatic and emphatic sibilants, with no change in meaning."}, {"id": "23:73/q03/p2", "position": "Pronounce ṣād with ishmām toward zāy, producing an intermediate sound.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER attests this pronunciation for Hamza and Khalaf."}]}
{"id": "23:73/q04", "question": "Why do the hearers turn away from the straight path?", "turns_on": "The notes variously attribute refusal to hostility to truth, failure to discern or reflect, ancestral loyalty, and disbelief in the Hereafter.", "positions": [{"id": "23:73/q04/p1", "position": "They hate the truth and obstinately resist a call whose objections have been answered.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi lists hatred of truth after the grounds for denial have been removed by 23:70-73. Al-Bursevi calls their refusal to follow or listen obstinate despite refutation from every angle. Al-Tabataba'i says those who hate truth turn away from the path to which the Prophet guides. Al-Zamakhshari's account, praised by al-Alusi, says they disliked the manifest truth and rejected the saving reminder despite miracles. Islahi says they acknowledge truth but contradict it and stray."}, {"id": "23:73/q04/p2", "position": "They lack discernment or fail to reflect on the evidence.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi presents lack of discernment as another explanation after the verses eliminate grounds for denial and accusation. Al-Zamakhshari, in the account praised by al-Alusi, exposes their failure to reflect although the Prophet was known to them, sought no payment or false distinction, and displayed truth and miracles."}, {"id": "23:73/q04/p3", "position": "Blind loyalty to ancestral ways keeps them from the call.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari, in the account praised by al-Alusi, includes blind ancestral loyalty among their failures."}, {"id": "23:73/q04/p4", "position": "Disbelief in the Hereafter causes them to evade and stray from the salvation path.", "reasons": "Asad says those who deny the afterlife deviate from the straight way. Islahi says following the path to the true destination requires belief in the Hereafter; hearts lacking that belief evade it and inevitably go astray."}]}
{"id": "23:73/q05", "question": "What reported illustrations explain the Prophet's call to this path?", "turns_on": "The reports use different events and images to portray guidance and responses to it.", "positions": [{"id": "23:73/q05/p1", "position": "Two angels liken him to a guide leading stranded travelers from barren ground toward gardens and water; some follow and some stay.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports Ibn Abbas's dream of the Prophet and his people, with two angels explaining the travelers and their guide."}, {"id": "23:73/q05/p2", "position": "The Prophet restrains his community from the Fire, but they rush toward it and some arrive at his Basin bearing misappropriated livestock.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports Umar's account of the Prophet's saying: he will disavow those with misappropriated livestock after delivering his message."}, {"id": "23:73/q05/p3", "position": "He invites a reluctant man to Islam by likening it to following a familiar guide from a rough route onto a broad, easy road.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports this parable from Qatada."}]}

{"id": "23:105/q01", "question": "What does the question do rhetorically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:105/q01/p1", "position": "It reproaches the condemned and reminds them that they denied recited signs, exposing the reason for their punishment and denying their excuse.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī places the rejected recitation in worldly life. {"id": "23:105/q03", "question": "What are 'My signs' here?", "turns_on": "Whether 'signs' names the Qur'an specifically, divine books or messages more broadly, warnings, or God's proofs and arguments.", "positions": [{"id": "23:105/q03/p1", "position": "They are the Qur'an or its verses recited to the people.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the Qur'an told them about the Day and its events. Al-Ṭabarī locates its recitation in worldly life. Al-Wāḥidī, reporting Muqātil and al-Kalbī, identifies the signs in the next verse as the Qur'an; his own explanation adds denial of the Qur'an and Muhammad concerning the Fire. Al-Baghawī says the Qur'an warned them. Al-Ṭabrisī offers the Qur'an as one reading. Al-Nasafī says they claimed it was not from God. Ibn ʿĀshūr points to the ordinary senses of 'recited to you' and 'you denied them.'"}, {"id": "23:105/q03/p2", "position": "They are God's books or conveyed messages.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports some exegetes saying God's books are recited to people. Asad calls them God's messages conveyed to the condemned."}, {"id": "23:105/q03/p3", "position": "They are warnings given to the people.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports this explanation from Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "23:105/q03/p4", "position": "They are God's proofs and arguments.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī offers this alongside the Qur'an as an explanation of the recited signs."}]}
{"id": "23:105/q04", "question": "Why are the signs attributed to God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:105/q04/p1", "position": "Attributing the signs to God presents them as possessing the highest rank.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī grounds their elevated description in their attribution to God."}]}
{"id": "23:105/q05", "question": "What does 'recited' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:105/q05/p1", "position": "It means read or recited.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites earlier uses of tilāwa in 2:102 and 8:2."}]}
{"id": "23:105/q06", "question": "What does the passive 'were recited' emphasize?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:105/q06/p1", "position": "The mere recitation of the signs should have sufficed to bring about belief.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī draws this point from the passive construction."}]}
{"id": "23:105/q07", "question": "What did their denial involve?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:105/q07/p1", "position": "They rejected the recited revelation in worldly life, persistently treating it as false.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies denial of what the Qur'an foretold about the Day. {"id": "23:105/q08", "question": "Why is 'in them' placed before 'you denied'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:105/q08/p1", "position": "The order emphasizes their persistent rejection of signs that should have led them to faith.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī reads the advance placement of 'in them' this way."}]}

{"id": "23:106/q05", "question": "How is شِقْوَتُنَا read and formed?", "turns_on": "The vowel of shīn and the presence of alif after qāf vary; the sources regard the principal nouns as equivalent while differing in their reader attributions.", "positions": [{"id": "23:106/q05/p1", "position": "Shiqwatunā: kasra on shīn, still qāf, and no alif.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī attributes it to most Medinans and Basrans and some Kufans; Ibn Mujāhid names Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim. Later sources call it the majority or Hijazi form. Ibn Khālawayh compares its pattern to fidya; al-Fārisī to ridda and fiṭna; al-Samīn to fiṭna and niʿma. Al-Farrāʾ cites a line with shaqwatihi as evidence. The two principal forms are synonymous verbal nouns; al-Ṭabarī accepts either, and a report says ʿĀṣim allowed both."}, {"id": "23:106/q05/p2", "position": "Shaqāwatunā: fatḥa on shīn and qāf, with an alif after qāf.", "reasons": "Most Kufans or Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī are named; al-Nashr and Ibn ʿĀshūr add Khalaf. Reports also name Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿmash, and others; transmissions from ʿĀṣim vary and permit both principal forms. It is a synonymous verbal noun, compared to saʿāda, salāma, or qasāwa; Qiraat-ER calls faʿāla common. Al-Farrāʾ cites Abū Tharwān's line for a hardship sense of this form."}, {"id": "23:106/q05/p3", "position": "Shaqwatunā: fatḥa on shīn with no alif and a still qāf.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī names ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, Abū Razīn, and Abū Rajāʾ; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī report it from Shibl."}, {"id": "23:106/q05/p4", "position": "Shiqāwatunā: kasra on shīn with an alif after qāf.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī report this variant from al-Ḥasan and Qatāda; al-Ālūsī specifies al-Ḥasan's transmission through Khālid ibn Ḥawshab."}, {"id": "23:106/q05/p5", "position": "Related nouns include shaqāʾ and shaqā, with long or short final vowel.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī records both usages; Abū Muslim compares shaqwa to the relation of jarya to flowing, so the noun can name a condition."}]}
{"id": "23:106/q06", "question": "What is the شِقْوَة that overcame them?", "turns_on": "The accounts identify different referents for misery: a prior decree, its final outcome, causes within desire and deeds, a moral attitude, or bad luck.", "positions": [{"id": "23:106/q06/p1", "position": "The wretched fate already decreed or written for them.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Muqātil, al-Quraẓī and others identify it with what was written. Al-Ṭabarī specifies prior knowledge and the Mother of the Book; Study Quran notes 43:4. Ibn Masʿūd says wretchedness is written in the womb, and Yaḥyā recalls a Prophetic report on happiness and wretchedness written there. The Ashʿarites identify the written matter as their disbelief and sins. Al-Ṭabarī's sinners cite it after rejected recitation."}, {"id": "23:106/q06/p2", "position": "Their desires and forbidden pleasures, which brought misery as their consequence.", "reasons": "Al-Jubbāʾī says they name the cause by its effect and admit responsibility. Al-Qurṭubī prefers this and cites 4:10, where consuming orphans' wealth is called eating fire. Al-Ṭabrisī calls neglecting God for idols and desire the gravest misery; al-Biqāʿī says desires led to evil deeds. Kur'an Yolu adds appetite, self-interest, and weakness rather than reasoned inquiry."}, {"id": "23:106/q06/p3", "position": "Their own evil deeds or acquired sinful disposition, which produced the bad end.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf says God knew their evil deeds deserved an evil outcome; al-Ṭabrisī says the deeds caused misery. Al-Nasafī calls their sinful deeds its cause, al-Būrsawī their bad choices, al-Ālūsī their bad disposition, and al-Ṣādiq their own deeds. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Ṭabāṭabāʾī stress voluntary choices; Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites their promise to do good if returned."}, {"id": "23:106/q06/p4", "position": "Misery as the opposite of happiness: an evil outcome, harm, or lost allotted good.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Jishumī define it by eventual harm versus benefit; al-Ṭabrisī says harm overtakes well-being. Al-Kashshāf says the bad end was known by God as deserved by their deeds, a gloss Rāzī repeats; al-Ālūsī attributes this view to most Muʿtazilites. Ṭabāṭabāʾī also offers the evil that characterizes them or lost allotted good. Abū Ḥayyān calls an evil outcome its ordinary sense."}, {"id": "23:106/q06/p5", "position": "Thinking well of oneself and badly of other people.", "reasons": "Abū Turāb gives the inward moral gloss; al-Māwardī, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Būrsawī transmit the same explanation. The reports vary slightly between 'bad opinion' generally and bad opinion of others."}, {"id": "23:106/q06/p6", "position": "The state of misery itself.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim derives shaqwa from shaqāʾ by analogy with jarya and flowing: the noun can denote a condition."}, {"id": "23:106/q06/p7", "position": "Misfortune that overwhelmed them during worldly life, leaving them unguided.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī specifies the time and result without specifying whether this misfortune was written or chosen."}, {"id": "23:106/q06/p8", "position": "Abstract bad luck, invoked as an excuse for their own failings.", "reasons": "Asad treats this contextual sense as the sinners' futile pretext."}]}

{"id": "23:106/q10", "question": "Is their statement a confession, excuse, or plea?", "turns_on": "The sources differ over whether naming misery functions as admission, pretext, or a factual causal statement.", "positions": [{"id": "23:106/q10/p1", "position": "It confesses culpability and the established proof against them, then leads into their plea for release.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls confession an apology and disavowal before the decreed command to be silent.
